Proof by Contradiction

Assume there are only finitely many primes and derive a contradiction. Watch a new prime slip outside the list.

Proof by contradiction assumes the opposite side. Push the false side until it clashes with itself. Then the original claim must be true. Multiplying all the primes and adding one builds that clash.

For example, suppose a biggest number exists. Add one and a bigger number appears. The assumption destroys itself. Euclid's prime proof uses exactly this move.

¬P  ⇒  ⊥  ⊢  P\lnot P \;\Rightarrow\; \bot \;\vdash\; P¬P⇒⊥⊢P

Examples & Exercises

Prove Euclid's theorem completely: there are infinitely many primes.

Use proof by contradiction — assume p1,…,pkp_1, \ldots, p_kp1​,…,pk​ are all the primes, and show that N=p1⋯pk+1N = p_1 \cdots p_k + 1N=p1​⋯pk​+1 (i) has a prime factor, since N≥2N \ge 2N≥2, and (ii) that this factor cannot equal any pip_ipi​, deriving a contradiction.

In particular, address the subtlety that NNN itself need not be prime (for k=6k = 6k=6, N=30031=59×509N = 30031 = 59 \times 509N=30031=59×509).

N=p1p2⋯pk+1,N≡1(modpi) for all iN = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1, \qquad N \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i} \ \text{for all } iN=p1​p2​⋯pk​+1,N≡1(modpi​) for all i
k=6:N=30031=59×509k = 6:\quad N = 30031 = 59 \times 509k=6:N=30031=59×509
Show proof

  1. We argue by contradiction.

    Suppose there are only finitely many primes — a complete list p1,…,pkp_1, \ldots, p_kp1​,…,pk​ (k≥1k \ge 1k≥1).

    Put P=p1⋯pkP = p_1 \cdots p_kP=p1​⋯pk​ and N=P+1N = P + 1N=P+1; then N≥3≥2N \ge 3 \ge 2N≥3≥2.

  2. Lemma: every integer ≥2\ge 2≥2 has a prime factor.

    Proof (strong induction): for n=2n = 2n=2, nnn itself is prime.

    For n>2n > 2n>2, either nnn is prime or n=abn = abn=ab with 1<a,b<n1 < a, b < n1<a,b<n; in the composite case the induction hypothesis gives aaa a prime factor qqq, and q∣a∣nq \mid a \mid nq∣a∣n, so qqq is a prime factor of nnn.

    Applying this to NNN yields a prime factor qqq of NNN.

  3. qqq differs from every pip_ipi​.

    Indeed, pi∣Pp_i \mid Ppi​∣P for each iii, so N=P+1≡1(modpi)N = P + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i}N=P+1≡1(modpi​): no pip_ipi​ divides NNN.

    But q∣Nq \mid Nq∣N, hence q≠piq \ne p_iq=pi​ for every iii.

    So qqq is a prime missing from the supposedly complete list — a contradiction.

    Hence there are infinitely many primes. ∎

  4. The subtlety: NNN itself need not be prime.

    For k=6k = 6k=6, P=2⋅3⋅5⋅7⋅11⋅13=30030P = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 = 30030P=2⋅3⋅5⋅7⋅11⋅13=30030 and N=30031=59×509N = 30031 = 59 \times 509N=30031=59×509 is composite.

    The proof is unaffected — its claim is "\emph{every} prime factor of NNN is new", not "NNN is a new prime".

    The proof does pin down that a new prime is among the factors of NNN, but identifying it requires factoring NNN.

Prove by contradiction that log⁡25\log_2 5log2​5 is irrational.

Hint: if log⁡25=pq\log_2 5 = \frac{p}{q}log2​5=qp​ with p,qp, qp,q positive integers, then 2p=5q2^p = 5^q2p=5q — the left side is even and the right side is odd.

log⁡25=pq  ⇒  5=2p/q  ⇒  5q=2p\log_2 5 = \frac{p}{q} \;\Rightarrow\; 5 = 2^{p/q} \;\Rightarrow\; 5^q = 2^plog2​5=qp​⇒5=2p/q⇒5q=2p
2p is even (p≥1),5q is odd2^p \text{ is even } (p \ge 1), \qquad 5^q \text{ is odd}2p is even (p≥1),5q is odd
Show proof

  1. We argue by contradiction.

    Suppose log⁡25\log_2 5log2​5 is rational.

    Since log⁡25>log⁡24=2>0\log_2 5 > \log_2 4 = 2 > 0log2​5>log2​4=2>0, we can write log⁡25=pq\log_2 5 = \frac{p}{q}log2​5=qp​ with p,qp, qp,q positive integers — in particular p≥1p \ge 1p≥1.

  2. By the definition of the logarithm, 5=2p/q5 = 2^{p/q}5=2p/q, and raising both sides to the power qqq gives 5q=2p5^q = 2^p5q=2p.

    But p≥1p \ge 1p≥1 makes 2p=2⋅2p−12^p = 2 \cdot 2^{p-1}2p=2⋅2p−1 even, while 5q5^q5q, a product of odd numbers, is odd.

    An even number cannot equal an odd number — a contradiction.

    Hence log⁡25\log_2 5log2​5 is irrational. ∎

  3. Note: there is no need to put pq\frac{p}{q}qp​ in lowest terms — the parity argument alone suffices. The deeper reason is the fundamental theorem of arithmetic (unique prime factorization): 2p2^p2p has only the prime factor 2 and 5q5^q5q only the prime factor 5, so the two powers with positive exponents can never agree.
